title: Cyber Resilience Act: can you still sell your products in the EU after 11 December 2027?
short: Report exploited flaws within 24 hours now, and give every product a risk assessment, SBOM, support period and CE marking by 11 December 2027.
answer: Be ready now to report an actively exploited vulnerability or severe incident in any product on the EU market within 24 hours. Before 11 December 2027, give every product a class, a support period, a risk assessment, an SBOM and technical documentation, so it can carry the CE marking.
audience: Companies that make, import or distribute hardware or software sold in the EU, and open-source stewards

blocks.title: If you only do five things

items.title: Be able to report within 24 hours.
items.text: Reporting has applied since 11 September 2026, also to products placed on the market before December 2027 and after their support ends[^guide]. Name an owner and a deputy with EU Login accounts and MFA, and decide which CSIRT you report to[^srpfaq].

items.title: Classify each product by its core functionality.
items.text: Match it against Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2392[^ir2392]. Default products may always self-assess; important and critical ones may need a notified body[^guide].

items.title: Set a support period per product.
items.text: Base it on expected use, comparable products and your components' own support, and make it at least 5 years unless use is shorter[^cra]. Show the end month and year at purchase[^cra].

items.title: Write the risk assessment first.
items.text: It decides how each Annex I requirement applies and goes into the technical documentation[^cra]. Cover planned features too, so the updates that add them aren't substantial modifications[^guide].

items.title: Run vulnerability handling as a process.
items.text: Due diligence on third-party and open-source components, an SBOM per release, a disclosure policy and contact, and free security updates[^cra]. The supply chain and secure development sheets show how.

blocks.title: Are you in scope, and in which role?

items.title: Does it connect to a device or network?
items.text: If so, the CRA covers it, with the remote data processing it needs to work[^cra]. Web apps used only in a browser, websites and SaaS are not products themselves[^guide].

items.title: Is it excluded?
items.text: Yes, if it's a medical or diagnostic device, a motor vehicle, a certified aviation product, marine equipment, an identical spare part or made only for national security or defense[^cra].

items.title: Do you supply it commercially?
items.text: Charging for it or for support beyond cost, monetizing it through other services or requiring personal data for more than security and compatibility counts, even if it's free[^cra]. Open source you don't monetize doesn't[^cra].

items.title: Are you an open-source steward?
items.text: You are if you're a foundation or company that systematically supports non-monetized open source meant for commercial use[^guide]. Stewards need a documented security policy[^cra], report from December 2027[^srpfaq] and can't be fined[^cra].

items.title: Which role do you have?
items.text: Manufacturers sell under their own name; importers and distributors check the CE marking and documents first[^cra]. Rebranding or substantially modifying a product makes you its manufacturer[^cra].

blocks.title: Product classes and conformity assessment
items: **Default.** Anything whose core functionality isn't in Annex III or IV. Self-assessment (module A) is always allowed[^guide].

**Important, class I.** 19 categories, such as identity and access management, browsers, password managers, antivirus, VPNs, operating systems, routers and smart home security products. Self-assess only by fully applying a cited harmonized standard, common specification or EU certificate at level substantial; otherwise use a notified body[^cra].
**Important, class II.** Hypervisors, container runtimes, firewalls, intrusion detection and prevention systems and tamper-resistant chips. Always third party[^cra].

**Critical.** Hardware security boxes, smart meter gateways and smartcards: EU certification where a delegated act requires it, otherwise as class II[^cra]. The class of the whole product counts, not that of its components[^guide].

**Check which standards are cited.** Only standards cited in the Official Journal give presumption of conformity[^cra]. ETSI's approval of its 17 product-specific drafts ends between mid-September and mid-November 2026, by product[^etsi].

blocks.title: Annex I in practice
items: **No known exploitable flaws at release.** Known means in the EU vulnerability database or another prominent one, or reported to you[^guide].
**Secure defaults.** A secure default configuration with a reset, access control, encryption of stored and transmitted data, minimal data and a way to delete it all[^cra].

**Automatic security updates on by default, where applicable.** With an opt-out, notifications and a way to postpone. Not required for components or where users don't expect them, as in industrial networks[^cra].

**An SBOM per release.** Machine-readable, covering at least top-level dependencies, and it needn't be public[^cra]. BSI TR-03183-2 asks for CycloneDX 1.6 or SPDX 3.0.1 or later, with dependencies resolved through everything you ship[^tr2].
**One contact point, not just a chatbot.** A single point of contact not limited to automated tools, plus a disclosure policy[^cra]. BSI's voluntary TR-03183-3 adds a signed `security.txt`[^tr3].

**Free fixes, kept available.** Keep each security update available for 10 years or the rest of the support period, if longer[^cra]. For software, fixing only the latest version is fine if upgrading costs users nothing extra[^cra].
**Advisories and upstream reports.** Publish fixed flaws, in CSAF as the BSI recommends[^cra][^tr3], and send component flaws to their maintainer[^cra].

blocks.title: Reporting clocks since 11 September 2026
blocks.intro: Clocks start at reasonable certainty after a prompt first check[^guide]. Report once on ENISA's platform, in Germany to CERT-Bund, and tell affected users[^cra][^bsisrp].

items.name: Actively exploited vulnerability
items.scope: Reliable evidence of exploitation[^cra]; a public exploit isn't enough[^bsisrp].

items.name: Severe incident
items.scope: It harms or could harm the product's protection of sensitive or important data or functions, or could plant malicious code in it or users' systems[^cra]. Ransomware at the maker counts only if it could affect the product, its updates or signing keys[^bsisrp].

blocks.title: Documentation, CE marking and fines
items: **Technical documentation (Annex VII).** Architecture, vulnerability handling with SBOM and disclosure policy, risk assessment, support period reasons, standards, test reports and the declaration. Keep it 10 years or for the support period, if longer[^cra].
**EU declaration of conformity.** Follow Annex V, ship it or a simplified version with its web address, and issue one for all EU acts that need one[^cra].
**CE marking from 11 December 2027.** On the product, or the packaging and declaration; for software, on the declaration or its website[^cra].

**Fines up to €15 million or 2.5% of worldwide turnover.** For breaching Annex I or Articles 13 and 14; €10 million or 2% for most other duties. Micro and small manufacturers aren't fined for a late 24-hour early warning, under Article 64(10) as corrected in July 2025[^cra][^cracorr].

blocks.title: What you can skip
items: **Waiting for harmonized standards.** The risk assessment, SBOM, disclosure policy and update channel don't depend on them.
**Reporting every vulnerable dependency.** Flaws that aren't reachable or exploited in your product aren't reportable; tell the maintainer[^guide].
**Redesigning products that already hold up.** Designs from before the CRA need no change if the risk assessment shows adequate measures[^guide].
**Registering on ENISA's platform early.** ENISA advises registering only when you first need to report[^srpfaq].

blocks.title: Mistakes that cost the most
items: **Counting on the transition for hardware.** Every unit placed on the market from 11 December 2027 must comply, even of an older model[^guide].
**Picking the wrong CSIRT.** The notification may be invalidated and need resubmitting[^srpfaq].
**Rebranding without noticing.** An importer or distributor selling under its own name becomes the manufacturer[^cra].
**A 5-year support period by reflex.** The Commission says 5 years is not a default; products used longer need longer support[^guide].

blocks.title: What changed in 2026
items: **Reporting went live on 11 September.** ENISA's platform is English only, has no API yet, and its 72-hour counter can show reports overdue early[^srpfaq].
**Draft Commission guidance, 27 July.** It explains scope, open source, substantial modification and support periods, and isn't binding[^guide].
**Germany is naming the BSI.** A bill the Bundestag passed on 15 October would make it market surveillance authority[^bthib][^brdrs].
**Radio equipment moves to the CRA.** The radio equipment cybersecurity delegated act is repealed from 11 December 2027[^dr339].

blocks.title: What this looks like at your size

columns.title: Small team, no security staff
items: List every product and version you sell in the EU, with its class and support end date.
Write a one-page runbook: who reports, to which CSIRT, from which EU Login accounts.
Work through BSI TR-03183-1 as a checklist[^tr].

columns.title: Growing, with IT or security staff
items: Name a product security owner and ship an SBOM and advisories with every release.
Plan for a notified body now if a product needs one; Member States aim to have enough by 11 December 2026[^cra].
Document one product end to end, then reuse it for its variants[^guide].

columns.title: Enterprise or regulated
items: Build module H on your ISO/IEC 27001 ISMS, as BSI TR-03183-H shows[^tr].
Run CRA reports in your NIS2 incident process; the EU security laws sheet has those clocks.
Agree how importers and distributors pass on the vulnerabilities they must report to you[^cra].

changes.text: Published after a copy edit and a source-by-source fact check, which confirmed the small-maker fines exemption in the July 2025 corrigendum, added component due diligence, a non-public SBOM and the Bundestag's 15 October vote, and separated BSI recommendations from CRA duties.
First draft, based on the CRA, Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2392, the Commission's draft guidance of July 2026, ENISA's reporting platform FAQ and the BSI's TR-03183 and reporting pages.
